nodes.front: Example 3 · Support: How does changing the values for (a), (h), and (k) transform the graph?
nodes.back: Listen for: (a) stretches and compresses the graph, (h) shifts the graph horizontally, and (k) shifts the graph vertically.

nodes.front: Example 3 · Connect representations: Compare and contrast the two functions shown in the graph.
nodes.back: Listen for: The graph of the parent function is wider. The graph of the transformed function is shifted below the (x)-axis. Both graphs are even, open upward, and are symmetrical across the (y)-axis.

nodes.front: Example 3 · Connect representations: Is the order in which you apply the transformations important?
nodes.back: Listen for: It doesn't matter in which order you apply the translations, but the vertical stretch should be applied before the vertical translation.

nodes.front: Example 3 · Connect representations: Why is knowing the graph of the parent function a valuable tool?
nodes.back: Listen for: Knowing the parent graph gives you a starting place. You do not have to make a table of points to graph the function; instead, you can compare the function to the parent function to determine the transformation.

nodes.front: Example 3 · Check student thinking: How does the graph of a function (g(x)=a(x-h)^n+k) compare to the graph of the parent function (f(x)=x^n)?
nodes.back: Listen for: The (a)-value stretches or compresses the graph vertically, the (h)-value shifts the graph horizontally, and the (k)-value shifts the graph vertically.
Provide an example that demonstrates the following statement is not true. If the degree of a function is an even number, then the function is an even function.
TE sample: f(x) = 2x^4 + x^3 - 2 has even degree but is not even: f(-x) = 2(-x)^4 + (-x)^3 - 2 = 2x^4 - x^3 - 2, which is not equal to f(x) (the TE prints the second f(x) where f(-x) is meant). …
Look at the polynomial graphs below: f(x) = x^2 (a parabola with vertex at the origin, both ends up) and g(x) = x^3 (through the origin, from lower left to upper right).

A. Is the graph of f or g symmetric about the y-axis? Is the graph of f or g symmetric about the origin? Explain. (f is symmetric about the y-axis: its reflection across the y-axis is identical; g is symmetric about the origin: it is identical when rotated 180 degrees about the origin.)

B. Look for Relationships: graph more functions of the form y = x^n where n is a natural number. Which of these functions are symmetric about the origin? Which are symmetric about the y-axis? What conjectures can you make? (Even n: symmetric about the y-axis; odd n: symmetric about the origin.)

What do you notice about the two graphs? → f(x) is a parabola that opens upward; it is symmetric across the y-axis and has a minimum at the origin. g(x) is cubic; it passes through the origin and it is symmetric about the origin.
What does it mean for a graph to be symmetrical? → It has an axis of symmetry; the graph is reflected across a line. One part of the graph is the mirror image of the other part.

Graph the functions m(x) = x and h(x) = x^4. How does the symmetry of these graphs compare to the symmetry of f(x) and g(x)? → The graph of m(x) is symmetric about the origin, like the graph of g(x). The graph of h(x) is symmetric about the y-axis, like the graph of f(x).

What do you notice about the degree of the polynomial and the type of symmetry it has? → A polynomial with an even degree is symmetric about the y-axis. A polynomial with an odd degree is symmetric about the origin.

nodes.front: Habits of Mind, Look for Relationships: ask?
nodes.back: Do you notice any other patterns among the functions with even degree and the functions with odd degree? → Functions with an even degree always go the same direction when approaching positive and negative infinity, while odd functions always go opposite directions.

The TE's After answer ('a polynomial with an even degree is symmetric about the y-axis') is true only for the power functions y = x^n on the screen, not for every polynomial; Practice 12 (the DOK 3 Extension) exists to break it. Say 'for y = x^n' on the board. …
